name: Centro de Arte Contemporáneo Wifredo Lam
funding: Art centre within the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP), a Ministry of Culture body. The Centre, CNAP and the Ministry co-sponsored the 15th Havana Biennial (2024 to 2025).
watch: Dutch funders Hivos and the Prince Claus Fund withdrew funds from its 2003 Biennial. An October 2021 open letter asked artists to boycott the 14th.
why_flagged: Art centre within the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP), a Ministry of Culture body. The Centre, CNAP and the Ministry co-sponsored the 15th Havana Biennial (2024 to 2025).
records_note: Its site (2014 archive) carries bulletins and Biennial pages and credits the Ministry of Culture and CNAP.
affiliations_note: Institution of the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP). Organises the Havana Biennial with CNAP.

overview: Contemporary art centre at Calle San Ignacio 22, corner of Empedrado, in Old Havana beside the Plaza de la Catedral (EcuRed).

Created on 28 February 1983 and named for the Cuban painter Wifredo Lam. Its purpose is to study and promote contemporary visual art from Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean and Lam's work, and to organise the Havana Biennial (EcuRed; CNAP).
Building: an 18th-century mansion of the Counts of Peñalver. A restoration was decided in 1984 and the building went to the Centre in 1993 (EcuRed).
The Biennial has run since 1984. Brasil de Fato reported that the 15th edition was scheduled to run to 28 February 2025 under director Nelson Ramírez de Arellano.
details.funding_verdict: Wifredo Lam Centre: mainly public: Ministry of Culture through CNAP, with foreign Biennial money withdrawn in 2003
funding: CNAP is a Ministry of Culture body created in 1989. Its page lists the Centre among the institutions that make up CNAP and says CNAP and the Centre organise the Biennial (CNAP, archive copy of 2023-12-08). Hyperallergic calls the Centre government-supported (2021).

Foreign funding: CNAP's president said in 2003 that foundations like Prince Claus and Hivos had provided 70 percent of the external funding for the previous Biennial. After the 2003 withdrawals the Cuban government agreed at the last minute to provide $156,000, less than first planned (IPS).

red_flags.heading: Funder withdrawal and boycotts aimed at the Havana Biennial
points: 2003: institutions from the Netherlands and France retracted funds pledged for the eighth Biennial (IPS, 2003-11-04). The Dutch groups Hivos and the Prince Claus Foundation were among them; France's AFAA, an agency of its foreign ministry, cited bureaucratic difficulties in allocating funds for artists travelling from Africa. CNAP president Rafael Acosta said foundations like Prince Claus and Hivos had retracted more than $200,000.

Hivos said censorship was evident in the programme. Prince Claus tied its decision to the March 2003 arrest of 75 dissidents and said it could not work with a Biennial whose organisers did not distance themselves from official policy (IPS).

Two artists, Alexander Apóstol of Venezuela and Priscila Moge of Costa Rica (spelling as in IPS), pulled out over disagreements about texts introducing their work. Acosta denied censorship in the cases a Venezuelan newspaper listed (IPS).
2015: several artists called for a boycott after the arrest of Tania Bruguera over a planned performance on free speech (Hyperallergic).

2021: on 2021-10-15 Cuban cultural workers published an open letter on e-flux asking colleagues not to join the 14th Biennial. By 2021-10-18 it had over 400 signatures and five participants had withdrawn (Hyperallergic).

press.overall: Criticism targets the Biennial the Centre runs, as funder withdrawals and boycott calls, not the Centre's exhibitions.

items.title: Valentina Di Liscia, "As Boycott of Havana Biennial Gains Steam, Artists Withdraw" (2021)
points: Reports five withdrawals and a boycott letter with over 400 signatures, and describes the Biennial as a state-sponsored show organised by the Centre since 1984.
Quotes Bruguera: Decrees 349, 370 and 35 remain in force, and parallel shows and critical works inside the Biennial failed, so a boycott is left.

items.title: Cuban cultural workers, "Open letter: Why we say NO to the 14th Havana Biennial and ask you to do the same" (2021)
points: Says Cuban artists have been in prison for months, dozens of cultural workers are under house arrest and over 1,000 people were arrested in the protests of 11 July, and that the organising institutions condoned and took part in the violence against cultural workers.
Does not name the Centre; it refers to "the institutions and functionaries that organize" the Biennial.

items.title: Dalia Acosta, "Arts Weekly / Cuba: Spectre of Censorship Haunts Biennial" (2003)
points: Reports the two artist withdrawals and the funding cuts by Dutch foundations, with France's AFAA citing bureaucratic difficulties, and Cuban officials' denials alongside.
Names the Wifredo Lam Centre as the recipient of one artist's complaint.

details.bottom_line: The Centre is paid by the Cuban state through CNAP, and no flagged funder was found in the sources opened. The weak points are documented protests aimed at the Biennial it runs: Dutch funders withdrew in 2003 and France's AFAA cited bureaucratic difficulties, and a boycott letter and five withdrawals followed in 2021. Worth watching: whether foreign funders or invited artists return for later editions.

name: Cinemateca de Cuba
funding: Film archive and cinema programme created in 1960 as a department of ICAIC, which sits in the Ministry of Culture. It moved into Alfredo Guevara's former house in October 2020.
watch: Member of the International Federation of Film Archives (FIAF). ICAIC, its parent, carries the censorship and protest flags.
records_note: The archive's site posts screening programmes by date range and a chronology of its history.

overview: Film archive and cinema programme of ICAIC, housed since October 2020 in the former home of Alfredo Guevara on calle 11 between 2 and 4 in Vedado, Havana (OnCuba).
The new seat was inaugurated on 20 October 2020, Cuban Culture Day, with President Miguel Díaz-Canel and ICAIC president Ramón Samada present (OnCuba).
Before the move it occupied the first floor of the ICAIC building (Spanish Wikipedia).
The Cinemateca's own chronology and EcuRed date its creation to 6 February 1960, as a cultural department of ICAIC. OnCuba names Héctor García Mesa as founder.

Spanish Wikipedia instead says Germán Puig founded a Cinemateca de Cuba in 1951 at the congress of the International Federation of Film Archives in Cambridge, citing a 2004 paper by Emmanuel Vincenot. EcuRed says an earlier film club used the name without holding a film collection and calls attributing the founding to it an error.

The new house holds bibliographic and press collections and a growing set of DVD and Blu-ray copies, a small hall called El Mégano for screenings and talks, and a large patio (OnCuba, quoting director Luciano Castillo).
It is a member of the International Federation of Film Archives (FIAF member list) and, per EcuRed, of the Latin American coordinator of moving image archives (CLAIM).
details.funding_verdict: Cinemateca de Cuba: state-funded: Ministry of Culture through ICAIC
funding: It is a department of ICAIC (its own chronology; EcuRed), and EcuRed lists ICAIC in the Ministry of Culture's system.
EcuRed states that ICAIC gives the Cinemateca a copy of each film it produces, and that private collections, purchases and donations of foreign films add to the holdings.
wider_context: OnCuba reports ICAIC, the Cinemateca's parent, as the body that dropped Regreso a Ítaca from the December 2014 Havana film festival, Santa y Andrés from the 2016 festival and Sueños al pairo from the 2020 Muestra Joven. Filmmakers answered with a statement in 2014, a public rejection in 2016 and withdrawn films in 2020 (OnCuba, 2015, 2016 and 2020).
The Cinemateca is a department of ICAIC.
details.bottom_line: The Cinemateca is a state archive inside ICAIC. The weak points are its parent's record of pulling films in 2014, 2016 and 2020, and the disagreement over its founding date: 1960 in EcuRed and its own chronology, 1951 in Spanish Wikipedia.

name: Festival Internacional del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano de La Habana
funding: Annual December festival organised by ICAIC, a Ministry of Culture body, since 1979. Its founder Alfredo Guevara chaired it until his death in 2013.
watch: In December 2023 the Asamblea de Cineastas Cubanos said Llamadas desde Moscú and La Habana de Fito were pulled. Regreso a Ítaca: 2014.
why_flagged: Annual December festival organised by ICAIC, a Ministry of Culture body, since 1979. Its founder Alfredo Guevara chaired it until his death in 2013.
records_note: Each year it opens a call for entries and announces its Premios Corales.
affiliations_note: Organised by ICAIC, which also runs the Cinemateca de Cuba and the Muestra Joven.

overview: Annual film festival in Havana. The first edition opened on 3 December 1979, convened by ICAIC, and its top prize is the Gran Premio Coral (Spanish Wikipedia).
Alfredo Guevara founded it and was its president until his death on 19 April 2013 (Spanish Wikipedia). Iván Giroud was its president in 2020.

It screens in Havana cinemas including Cine 23 y 12, Chaplin, Riviera, Yara, La Rampa, Acapulco and Infanta, and in the Sala Glauber Rocha of the Fundación del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano (Prensa Latina).
The 42nd edition was split in two: 3 to 13 December 2020 and 11 to 21 March 2021 (Spanish Wikipedia).

Prensa Latina said the 46th edition closed on 14 December 2025 after 283 screenings, with more than 2,000 works submitted and 114 productions selected, dedicated to Guevara's centenary with Mexico as guest of honour. These are the agency's figures.
details.funding_verdict: Festival Internacional del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano de La Habana: state-funded through ICAIC and the Ministry of Culture
funding: ICAIC organises the festival (Spanish Wikipedia), and EcuRed lists ICAIC in the Ministry of Culture's system.
In December 2025 Prensa Latina reported a film-creation fellowship for women over 50, launched in collaboration with the UN Population Fund.

red_flags.heading: State censorship or punishment
points: December 2014: the 36th festival dropped Laurent Cantet's Regreso a Ítaca. Twelve filmmakers said the highest authorities of the Ministry of Culture and ICAIC forced the festival's directors to withdraw it, although it had been printed in the catalogue under the section Entornos (OnCuba, 13 April 2015).
2016: ICAIC dropped Carlos Lechuga's Santa y Andrés after it was preselected to compete at the 38th festival, according to the director Fernando Pérez (OnCuba, 8 December 2016).

red_flags.heading: Protest or boycott
points: December 2014: twelve filmmakers issued the statement "No ha de temerse la sinceridad" (translation: Sincerity need not be feared) against the withdrawal of Regreso a Ítaca, aimed at the Ministry of Culture and ICAIC leaders. National Film Prize winners including Leo Brouwer, Julio García Espinosa and Fernando Pérez later joined it (OnCuba).
December 2016: Fernando Pérez publicly called the exclusion of Santa y Andrés from the festival an error (OnCuba).

press.overall: Two OnCuba pieces report on films dropped from the festival's programme and the protests that followed; they criticise those decisions, not the festival's selection as a whole.

items.title: Cecilia Crespo, "Regreso a Ítaca podrá verse en La Habana" (2015)
points: Says the film was pulled from the official programme on an unconvincing pretext about fit with the festival's sections, and calls it an evident case of censorship for non-artistic reasons.

items.title: Ángel Marqués Dolz, "Fernando Pérez: 'La libertad es la única vía'" (2016)
points: Pérez says Santa y Andrés was preselected for the 38th festival and then discarded by ICAIC, and calls a policy of exclusion unsustainable.

details.bottom_line: The festival is a state event run by ICAIC; Prensa Latina reported a 2025 fellowship launched with the UN Population Fund. The weak points are the 2014 and 2016 film withdrawals and the public objections to them.

name: Festival Internacional Jazz Plaza
funding: Annual January jazz festival first held in 1980 and organised by the Instituto Cubano de la Música. The 42nd edition is set for 24 to 31 January 2027.
watch: Holguín was announced as a venue for the 41st edition (Prensa Latina, November 2025). Organisers say over 120 US artists have confirmed for 2027.
records_note: Each year organisers present a poster, spot and theme song at a press conference.
affiliations_note: Organised by the Instituto Cubano de la Música, part of the Ministry of Culture system. The 41st edition used the Sala Avellaneda of the Teatro Nacional de Cuba, per EcuRed.

overview: Annual jazz festival in Havana with sub-venues in other provinces, organised by the Instituto Cubano de la Música (EcuRed). Prensa Latina names Indira Fajardo as president of the institute and Víctor Rodríguez as president of the festival.
Began in 1980 from jam sessions at the Casa de la Cultura of the Plaza municipality, organised by the musician Bobby Carcassés, whom an EFE text carried by 14ymedio in 2024 calls its founding father.

The 40th edition ended on 2 February 2025 with about 300 shows (14ymedio). The 41st ran from 25 January to 1 February 2026: Prensa Latina, a state agency, announced on 7 November 2025 that Holguín joined for the first time and on 1 February 2026 listed it among the festival's venues. EcuRed says the edition opened at the Sala Avellaneda of the Teatro Nacional.

The 42nd edition is set for 24 to 31 January 2027, dedicated to dance, with 20 stages in Havana and activities in Santiago de Cuba, Holguín, Camagüey, Villa Clara and Matanzas, plus a sub-venue at the Centro Cultural México-Cuba Benny Moré in Mexico City (teleSUR).
Venues have included the Teatro Nacional, the Teatro Martí and Fábrica de Arte Cubano, which is a separate pin on the atlas (EFE via 14ymedio, 2024).
details.funding_verdict: Festival Internacional Jazz Plaza: mainly public: Ministry of Culture, through the Instituto Cubano de la Música
funding: The Instituto Cubano de la Música belongs to the Ministry of Culture system (EcuRed). EFE, in a 14ymedio piece of January 2024, says the festival has been coordinated by the Centro Nacional de Música Popular, the Instituto and the Ministry of Culture.
Organisers say more than 120 US artists have confirmed for 2027 and that by November 2025, 220 international artists and young Cubans abroad had confirmed for 2026 (teleSUR, Prensa Latina).

press.overall: One opinionated report from an independent outlet critical of the government; it concerns absent musicians and a cancelled film screening.

items.title: José Lassa, "Termina el Festival Jazz Plaza y la noche habanera vuelve a quedar en silencio" (2025)
points: Calls the festival, once more, a festival of the absent: Chucho Valdés, Arturo Sandoval and Paquito D'Rivera, all exiled in the United States, were missing from the Irakere tribute, and Cuban jazz is more alive abroad than at home.

Reports that the organisers suspended the screening of Pavel Giroud's documentary "Manteca, mondongo y bacalao con pan", planned for the Saturday before the close. Giroud, who lives abroad, remarked ironically that the organisers had changed their minds about programming it.
Names the organisers.

details.bottom_line: The festival is organised by the state's Instituto Cubano de la Música, and no flagged funder was found. The weak points are the 2025 cancellation of a documentary screening, which 14ymedio reports, and the absence of exiled musicians that 14ymedio describes. Worth watching: sponsors of the 2027 edition.

name: Gran Teatro de La Habana Alicia Alonso
funding: State theatre run by the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas, under the Ministry of Culture. Reopened in 2016 after a three-year restoration; new repairs were under way in 2025.
watch: Home of the Ballet Nacional de Cuba. The council's president named roof, air-conditioning and vibration damage behind the 2025 repair.
records_note: The council's president explained the 2025 repair on Canal Habana's magazine programme.
affiliations_note: Run by the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas, which also runs the Teatro Nacional de Cuba. Home of the Ballet Nacional de Cuba and the Teatro Lírico Nacional's opera seasons.

overview: Theatre complex on the block bounded by San Rafael, San José, Consulado and the Paseo del Prado in Havana (EcuRed).
The Centro Gallego bought the site in 1906 for its social palace, built to designs by the Belgian architect Paul Beleu. The Teatro Tacón, officially opened in 1838, had stood there before (EcuRed).
It has been the permanent home of the Ballet Nacional de Cuba since 1965 and also houses the Teatro Lírico Nacional and the Ballet Español de Cuba (EcuRed).
The Council of State renamed it for the ballerina Alicia Alonso in September 2015 (EcuRed; EFE in Diario las Américas).

A three-year restoration ended with a reopening on 1 January 2016, attended by President Raúl Castro and Alonso. EFE reported a renovated main hall, the García Lorca, seating 1,300, plus a new café and a small performance space.

New repair work was under way in October 2025, when Lillitsy Hernández Oliva, president of the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas, named air-conditioning leaks, a deteriorated third-floor roof and damage from sound vibrations (Periódico Cubano, citing the Canal Habana programme Hola Habana).
details.funding_verdict: Gran Teatro de La Habana Alicia Alonso: state-funded: Ministry of Culture through the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas
funding: The Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas (CNAE) runs the theatre; EcuRed lists it among the council's institutions and lists the council in the Ministry of Culture's system.

Culture Minister Julián González described the three-year restoration at the reopening (EFE). Periódico Cubano calls the 2013 to 2015 capital repair a multimillion investment covering façades, lobbies, boxes, roofs, stage floors, air-conditioning, acoustics, more than 20 dressing rooms and a recording studio.

press.overall: Two news reports describe repeated decay, and one asks where repair money went; neither is art criticism.

items.title: Periódico Cubano, "Cubanos tras reparación del Gran Teatro de La Habana: '¿Otra vez? Se robaron los recursos'" (2025)
points: Reports new repairs less than a decade after the 2016 reopening, for structural and termite damage, and says the work has drawn criticism of management and the use of public money.
Unverified: social media users quoted by the paper say the money for the earlier repair was stolen.
Calls for more transparent and efficient management.

items.title: Juan Diego Rodriguez (14ymedio), "Electrocution Risk from Leaks at Havana's National Theater" (2023)
points: Quotes a bassoonist who said in March 2023 that the Gran Teatro and the Karl Marx Theater were closed because of termites.
Mostly about the Teatro Nacional.

details.bottom_line: This is a state theatre paid by the Ministry of Culture through the CNAE. The weak point is a second major repair within a decade of the 2016 reopening.

name: Instituto Cubano del Arte e Industria Cinematográficos (ICAIC)
funding: State film body created by Law No. 169 in 1959, funded through the Ministry of Culture. It runs the Cinemateca, the Havana film festival, the Muestra Joven and animation studios.
watch: Films pulled: Regreso a Ítaca 2014, Santa y Andrés 2016, Sueños al pairo 2020. In 2023 the Asamblea de Cineastas Cubanos denounced ICAIC censorship.
why_flagged: State film body created by Law No. 169 in 1959, funded through the Ministry of Culture. It runs the Cinemateca, the Havana film festival, the Muestra Joven and animation studios.
records_note: ICAIC's Cubacine site carries the quarterly magazine Cine Cubano, the monthly paper Cartelera Cine y Video and calls for its Fondo de Fomento del Cine Cubano.
affiliations_note: Part of the Ministry of Culture system. Runs the Cinemateca de Cuba, the Havana film festival, the Muestra Joven, animation studios and the national film distributor.

overview: State film body in Havana, created by Law No. 169 of the Council of Ministers, made public on 24 March 1959 over the signatures of Prime Minister Fidel Castro and Education Minister Armando Hart. Alfredo Guevara was its first president (EcuRed).
ICAIC's own site says Guevara wrote its creation law and presided over it for thirty years.

EcuRed calls it the national film authority and main producer of feature films, documentaries and animation, and says it also runs the Cinemateca de Cuba, film archives, festivals and film distribution.
It organises the Havana film festival, first held on 3 December 1979 (Spanish Wikipedia).
Its president was Ramón Samada in 2020 (OnCuba) and Alexis Triana in 2025 (EcuRed).
details.funding_verdict: Instituto Cubano del Arte e Industria Cinematográficos (ICAIC): state-funded through the Ministry of Culture
funding: EcuRed lists ICAIC in the Ministry of Culture's system. The Ministry was created in 1976 (EcuRed; Spanish Wikipedia gives December 1976), 17 years after ICAIC.
EcuRed lists a Fondo de Fomento department in its central office.

red_flags.heading: State censorship or punishment
points: Regreso a Ítaca, December 2014: the 36th Havana festival, which ICAIC organises, dropped Laurent Cantet's film, based on Leonardo Padura's novel and shot in Havana. Twelve Cuban filmmakers said the highest authorities of the Ministry of Culture and ICAIC forced the festival's directors to withdraw it. The film had been printed in the festival catalogue (OnCuba, 13 April 2015).
Santa y Andrés, 2016: ICAIC dropped Carlos Lechuga's film after it was preselected for the 38th Havana festival, according to the director Fernando Pérez (OnCuba, 8 December 2016).

Sueños al pairo, February 2020: ICAIC removed the documentary on the musician Mike Porcel, by José Luis Aparicio Ferrera and Fernando Fraguela Fosado, from the Muestra Joven. The Muestra's board said the ICAIC presidency censored it for political and ideological differences and denied its authors the right to use archive images; Aparicio said ICAIC objected to its treatment of the Mariel exodus. ICAIC then postponed the 19th Muestra Joven (OnCuba, 27 February 2020).

Quiero hacer una película, 2018: ICAIC moved Yimit Ramírez's unfinished film to a 24-seat room and he withdrew it; ICAIC's leadership then stated the institution's right to make its own decisions (OnCuba, 27 February 2020).

red_flags.heading: Protest or boycott
points: December 2014: twelve filmmakers issued a statement titled "No ha de temerse la sinceridad" (translation: Sincerity need not be feared), aimed at the Ministry of Culture and ICAIC leaders over Regreso a Ítaca. The National Film Prize winners Leo Brouwer, Julio García Espinosa, Daysi Granados, Eslinda Núñez, Juan Padrón, Manuel Pérez, Fernando Pérez, Raúl Pérez Ureta, Enrique Pineda Barnet and Juan Carlos Tabío later joined it (OnCuba).
December 2016: Fernando Pérez publicly called the veto on Santa y Andrés an error and said a policy of exclusion was unsustainable (OnCuba).

February 2020: directors Daniela Muñoz Barroso, Regis Guedes, Carla Valdés León, Carlos Lechuga (with Marcos Castillo), Josué García Gomez and Marcos Alejandro Yglesias Ravelo withdrew their films from the Muestra Joven in response to the removal of the documentary; Aparicio left the Muestra's board (OnCuba).

press.overall: OnCuba reported the three film withdrawals of 2014, 2016 and 2020 and the filmmakers' protests; the pieces criticise ICAIC's decisions, not its films.

items.title: Cecilia Crespo, "Regreso a Ítaca podrá verse en La Habana" (2015)
points: Calls the film's removal from the festival programme a case of evident censorship for non-artistic reasons.
Reports that it would screen at the French Film Festival from 30 April 2015; Padura said negotiations with ICAIC and the Ministry since December had helped.

items.title: Ángel Marqués Dolz, "Fernando Pérez: 'La libertad es la única vía'" (2016)
points: Pérez, speaking at the launch of issue 200 of ICAIC's magazine Cine Cubano, said the veto was an error because nothing can be silenced now.

items.title: Redacción OnCuba, "Posponen Muestra Joven de cine; realizadores retiran sus obras tras la censura de un documental" (2020)
points: Reports ICAIC's note that it postponed the Muestra to create better conditions and that it backs the Muestra and young filmmakers.

details.bottom_line: ICAIC is a state body paid through the Ministry of Culture. The weak points are the film withdrawals of 2014, 2016 and 2020, each followed by public objections from filmmakers.

name: Museo Castillo del Morro San Pedro de la Roca
funding: Cuban state property; UNESCO names the Consejo Nacional del Patrimonio Cultural as responsible agency. A museum opened in the fortress on 23 July 1978. State bodies began repairs in 2020.
watch: UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997. Granma, quoted by OnCuba in April 2021, reported the repairs would continue through 2021.
records_note: UNESCO's listing text names the owner and the responsible national agency.
affiliations_note: UNESCO names the Consejo Nacional del Patrimonio Cultural (Ministry of Culture) as the responsible national agency. The Centro Provincial de Patrimonio Cultural de Santiago de Cuba took part in the 2020 to 2021 repairs (Granma via OnCuba).

overview: Fortress at the entrance of Santiago de Cuba's bay, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1997 under criteria iv and v, on a 93.88-hectare property (UNESCO, archived copy of 2 January 2025).

Construction began in 1638 on designs by the Italian military engineer Juan Bautista Antonelli (EcuRed, UNESCO). The governor Pedro de la Roca y Borjas started the stone fortress, an English attack destroyed it in 1662 and it was rebuilt between 1663 and 1669 (EcuRed).

Used as a military prison during the independence war. Emilio Bacardí Moreau was among the prisoners (EcuRed, Havana Times). The US army occupied it after 1898 and in 1904 it was registered as Cuban state property (EcuRed).
Restored from 1962 under Francisco Prat Puig. A museum opened inside on 23 July 1978 (EcuRed). UNESCO calls it the Museo de la Piratería and says it has occupied the castle since 1978.
Designated a National Monument by Commission resolutions 9/1979 and 147/1997 (UNESCO).
UNESCO noted conservation problems in 1997, mainly degraded wooden elements, eroded walls and plant growth.
details.funding_verdict: Museo Castillo del Morro San Pedro de la Roca: public: Cuban state property, managed by the provincial heritage centre
funding: UNESCO states that the Cuban state owns the castle, that the responsible national agency is the Consejo Nacional del Patrimonio Cultural, and that the Centro Provincial del Patrimonio Cultural de Santiago de Cuba manages it.

Repairs: Granma, quoted by OnCuba in April 2021, reported that works begun in 2020 by the Oficina del Conservador, the provincial heritage centre, the monuments restoration company and other local bodies focused on the main bridge, replacing wooden parts with a hard timber, and would continue through 2021.
not_related: the Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro in Havana and the Castillo de San Felipe del Morro in San Juan, Puerto Rico. EcuRed names them as sister fortifications of the Caribbean; they are separate sites.
details.bottom_line: The castle is Cuban state property run through the Ministry of Culture's heritage system, and no flagged funder was found. The 2020 to 2021 repairs rest on a Granma account quoted by OnCuba. Worth watching: repair funding and any UNESCO monitoring of the wooden elements.

name: Museo de Arte Colonial
funding: Its operator, the Office of the City Historian of Havana (Dirección de Patrimonio Cultural), runs on the state budget and other authorised sources (Decree-Law 368, 2018).
watch: Opened 30 July 1969 in the 1720 Casa Bayona on Plaza de la Catedral.
why_flagged: Opened 30 July 1969 in the 1720 Casa Bayona on Plaza de la Catedral.
records_note: The Historian's Office page describes collections and the annex.
affiliations_note: Run by the Office of the City Historian of Havana, with an annex in the Palacio de Lombillo.

overview: Museum of colonial furniture and decorative art in a house at San Ignacio 61, facing the Plaza de la Catedral in Old Havana (Spanish Wikipedia; Historian's Office).
Opened on 30 July 1969. In 1963 the National Commission of Museums and Monuments had restored the house (Historian's Office).

Building: a house dated 1720 that belonged to Luis Chacón, three times military governor of Cuba. It is also called Casa Bayona or Palacio de los Condes de Casa Bayona (Historian's Office; Spanish Wikipedia; OnCuba).
From 1856 the house held the Real Colegio de Escribanos, the newspaper La Discusión and the Arechabala liquor firm (Historian's Office).

On show: furniture, decorative arts, architectural elements, Cuban stained glass and colonial transport, with furnished rooms that recreate noble houses, and a room for temporary shows. OnCuba counts four rooms, three permanent.
An annex in the Palacio de Lombillo, at Empedrado 151, shows a collection of tableware (Historian's Office).
Old Havana is a UNESCO World Heritage site, listed on 14 December 1982 (Historian's Office).
details.funding_verdict: Museo de Arte Colonial: mainly public: Office of the City Historian, on the state budget and other authorised sources
funding: Decree-Law 368 of 2018 (Gaceta Oficial No. 24, 2019-04-03) says the Historian's Office system works from the State budget and other authorised funding, answers to the Council of Ministers, can receive donations, and can hold bank accounts in national and convertible currency.
The Office says Decree-Law 143 of 1993 let it create its own income sources, and that museum entrance fees and shop sales added to its funds (Historian's Office, archive copy of 2017).
details.bottom_line: The museum is paid by the Cuban state through the Historian's Office, which also keeps ticket and shop income, and no flagged funder was found in the sources opened. Worth watching: published accounts for the Office's museums, and the source of the donations the Office is allowed to receive.

name: Museo de la Revolución
funding: Created 12 December 1959 by decree of the Revolutionary Armed Forces Ministry (MINFAR) and housed in the former presidential palace since 1974.
watch: The Granma yacht stands in a memorial in its grounds. Decree No. 17 was signed by Raúl Castro as MINFAR minister.
records_note: MINFAR, the armed forces ministry, created it by decree; its 2014 pages on the heritage council site list hours and dollar ticket prices only.
affiliations_note: Runs the Granma Memorial in its grounds, built in 1976 as an annex.

propaganda.summary: Created on 12 December 1959 by a decree of the Ministry of the Revolutionary Armed Forces signed by Raúl Castro. Installed in the former Presidential Palace in 1974 to present the Revolution's history.

overview: History museum in the former Presidential Palace in Old Havana, on Refugio between Avenida de las Misiones and Zulueta (EcuRed).

Created on 12 December 1959 by Decree No. 17 of the Revolutionary Armed Forces minister, Raúl Castro (EcuRed). Prensa Latina calls it a decree of the Ministry of the Revolutionary Armed Forces (MINFAR), signed by Castro as minister. It first sat in the Castillo de la Punta and the base of the José Martí monument, and moved into the palace on 4 January 1974 (EcuRed; Prensa Latina).
Its first collection was material gathered by Celia Sánchez Manduley, a fighter of the 26th of July Movement (Prensa Latina).

Building: put up from 1909 as the seat of Havana's provincial government. President Mario García Menocal took it as the national executive's seat in 1917, and the Presidency and Council of Ministers sat there until 1965. Architects were Rodolfo Maruri and Paul Belau, and Tiffany Studios did the interiors (EcuRed; Prensa Latina).
The Granma Memorial in the grounds, opened on 1 December 1976, holds the yacht Granma, a T-34 tank, two historic aircraft and the turbine of a US U-2 shot down on 27 October 1962 (EcuRed).
Declared a National Monument in 2010 (Prensa Latina).
Claims from state sources: Prensa Latina says about nine thousand pieces and over 30 rooms, and EcuRed says over 300,000 visitors a year, nearly half foreign.
Visiting: EcuRed lists opening every day from 10:00 to 17:00.
details.funding_verdict: Museo de la Revolución: state museum: created in 1959 by decree of the armed forces ministry (MINFAR)
funding: Prensa Latina and EcuRed both say MINFAR created it in 1959. An archive copy of 2013 shows its page in the museums section of the National Council of Cultural Heritage website; the Council is a Ministry of Culture body (Spanish Wikipedia).

MINFAR is on the US State Department's Cuba Restricted List, under "Ministries": in the initial list published in the Federal Register as document 2017-24449 (Public Notice 10195), effective 2017-11-09, and in the version on the State Department's list page dated as of 2025-07-14. Both texts say entities owned or controlled by a listed entity are not restricted unless named.
details.bottom_line: The armed forces ministry created the museum in 1959 and is on the US Cuba Restricted List. The list names MINFAR, not the museum, and no source opened says MINFAR funds the museum now or names any other funder. Its visitor and collection figures come from state media and are claims. Worth watching: which body funds and directs the museum today.

name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes de La Habana
funding: State museum subordinate to Cuba's Ministry of Culture. Gilbert Brownstone gave nine works in January 2010 and pledged 120.
watch: The October 2021 boycott letter targets the Havana Biennial and the government, not this museum.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
records_note: Its who-we-are page gives only a mission.
finances_note: Restoration of the three-building complex, 2001: original budget estimate 31 million Cuban pesos, about 40 percent in foreign currency (Prensa Latina's Cuba Internacional, via IPS, 17 July 2001).
affiliations_note: Part of Cuba's National Museum System, which the Ministry of Culture directs through the Consejo Nacional de Patrimonio Cultural (Law 106, 2009). Runs the Palacio de Bellas Artes (Cuban art) and the Palacio del Centro Asturiano (international art).

overview: Cuba's national fine arts museum, split between two buildings in central Havana: the Palacio de Bellas Artes for Cuban art and the Palacio del Centro Asturiano for universal art.
Decreed on 23 February 1913 by President José Miguel Gómez and opened on 28 April 1913 as the Museo Nacional de la República (Spanish Wikipedia). The director is Jorge Fernández Torres.

Palacio de Bellas Artes: designed by Alfonso Rodríguez Pichardo and opened on 18 June 1954 on the former site of the Mercado de Colón. Palacio del Centro Asturiano: designed by Manuel del Busto, opened in 1927 as the Centro Asturiano's seat. The universal collections have been there since 2001.

Collection: about 47,600 pieces, of which 45,000 are part of the artistic heritage, including Cuban art, European painting and sculpture, and Egyptian, Greek and Roman antiquities (Spanish Wikipedia).
Visiting: Spanish Wikipedia lists 09:00 to 17:00 Wednesday to Saturday and 09:00 to 14:00 Sunday.
details.funding_verdict: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes de La Habana: mainly public: the Cuban state, under the Ministry of Culture
funding: Spanish Wikipedia describes the museum as public and under the Ministry of Culture.
The same article records a 14.5 million dollar renovation from 1996 (payer not stated) and a 2010 donation of more than 120 works by the Brownstone Foundation.

red_flags.heading: Artists' protest delivered to the museum, 2021
points: 24 May 2021: Cuban artists aligned with the activist group 27N asked the museum's director, Jorge Fernández, to cover their works on view and to take their works not on display off the museum's web page. They set three conditions: Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara returned home, his wellbeing verified by friends and family, and the police siege against him since November 2020 ended (The Art Newspaper, which says "Museum of Fine Arts" and names no artists).

25 May 2021: OnCuba, which names the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, listed seven signatories (Tania Bruguera, Tomás Sánchez, Marco Castillo, Jorge Luis Marrero, Sandra Ceballos, Celia-Yunior, Reynier Leyva Novo) and said they delivered the letter in person to Fernández Torres.
The protest concerned the treatment of Otero Alcántara. Neither The Art Newspaper nor OnCuba reports any response from the museum.

press.overall: Little criticism of the museum itself in art media. The main case is the 2021 artists' withdrawal request; one other piece criticises state cultural policy around the museum.

items.title: Daniel Cassady, "Cuban artists ask Museum of Fine Arts to remove their work from display while Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara remains in government custody" (2021)
points: Reports the request of artists aligned with 27N to the director, tied to Otero Alcántara's treatment after his hunger strike against government restrictions on artistic freedom; the government's official response, as 27N's letter reports it, is that he "is neither detained nor prosecuted".
Refers to the "Museum of Fine Arts" in Havana and its director Jorge Fernández; it does not use the museum's full name.

items.outlet: The New York Review of Books
items.title: Esther Allen, "The Art of the Possible at Havana's Bienal" (2019)
points: Describes the museum as host of the two central exhibitions of the 13th Bienal; one was curated by Fernández Torres.
Reports that Bruguera declined to attend, saying the Ministry of Culture was diverting resources to the Bienal to "whitewash its international image" after Decree 349.
Criticises the Bienal and the decree more than the museum.

wider_context: Decree 349, signed in April 2018 by Miguel Díaz-Canel, requires artists to obtain government approval before exhibiting; Esther Allen (NYRB, 2019) calls it the legal basis for the arrest of Otero Alcántara and other artists.

An open letter published by e-flux on 15 October 2021 asked the art community to boycott the 14th Havana Biennial, stating that Cuban artists have been in prison for months and dozens of cultural workers are under house arrest. It does not name the museum.
The museum is connected through the 2019 Bienal: it hosted the central exhibitions, one curated by its own director.
details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum is Cuban state money, with no private funder named. The weak points are the artists' 2021 protest to its director, which drew no reported answer, and its role as venue for state-promoted Bienal shows under a censorship decree. Worth watching is whether its website returns with reports or accounts.
